subject: sociology
title: Beliefs in Society: Religion's Role
welcome_lead: Conservative force, ideology or engine of change? Theorists disagree.
meta_desc: A-Level Sociology beliefs: religion as conservative force, ideology, change Weber Marx.
final_note: Religion does many things — depending on whose lens you use.

concepts.def: Religion creates social solidarity and shared values.
Marx — opium of the masses, false consciousness.
Religion mobilising poor for change (Latin America 1960s).
Feminist critique — male gods, female subordination.

walkthroughs.body_html: Durkheim (1912): religion separates sacred from profane. The Arunta totem was 'society worshipping itself'. Parsons (1965): religion answers existential questions and reinforces values. Bellah (1967): US civil religion unites citizens via flag, presidency, anthem.

Marx (1844): religion is 'the opium of the people', easing suffering and justifying inequality via promises of afterlife. Lenin extended this — religion is spiritual gin distracting workers. Feminists (Daly 1973) add patriarchy — male god, all-male clergy, control of women's reproduction.

Weber (1905) 'The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism': Calvinist beliefs in predestination drove ascetic hard work and reinvestment, sparking rational capitalism. Religion can create change. Bruce (2003): black US civil rights drew strength from black churches.

mcqs.q: What do feminists mean by the 'dark side' of family life?
options: The 'dark side' refers to families who live in poverty.
Humans need no social input to develop normally.
The 'dark side' is a metaphor about families who don't communicate.

The reality that families can be sites of inequality, exploitation and violence — particularly affecting women and children — challenging functionalist portrayals of the family as universally beneficial.
